questions.question: Why should you never tune hyperparameters based on test set performance?
options: Adjusting the model based on test results effectively trains on the test set, making the reported performance meaningless
The test set is generally too small in most real-world datasets to give reliable performance estimates at all
Hyperparameters cannot legally be changed once a model has finished its initial training run
The test set always contains different features than the training set entirely, so any comparison between the two is invalid
questions.explanation: Every time you adjust your model based on test performance, you leak test information into your modeling decisions. The test set must be used exactly once at the end for an unbiased estimate.

questions.question: A dataset has 95% negative and 5% positive samples. A model predicts 'negative' for every sample. What is its accuracy?
options: 50%, the random-guess baseline you'd expect for a balanced two-class problem
5%, equal to the positive-class rate since the model misses every positive sample
95%, since predicting the majority class every time gets every negative sample right
0%, since a model that never predicts positive should score no better than random chance
questions.explanation: Accuracy = correct predictions / total = 950/1000 = 95%. This shows why accuracy is misleading for imbalanced data -- a useless model looks great.

questions.question: In K-fold cross-validation with K=5, how many times is each data point used for validation?
options: 5 times, once for every fold, since each fold reuses the full dataset for validation purposes
It depends entirely on which random seed was used to shuffle the data before it gets split into the five folds
Never -- with K-fold CV all data is reserved for training and no data is ever held out for validation
Exactly once, since each of the K folds serves as the validation set for one round and training data the rest
questions.explanation: In K-fold CV, data is split into K equal folds. Each fold is used as the validation set exactly once while the remaining K-1 folds are used for training.

questions.question: A learning curve shows training score = 0.95 and validation score = 0.60 that does not improve with more data. What should you try?
options: Collect more training data, since a wider validation gap always means the model just hasn't seen enough examples
Use a simpler model or add regularization to reduce variance, since this is a classic overfitting signature
Remove the validation set entirely so the model can train on all of the available data instead
Increase the learning rate so the model converges to a better optimum more quickly than before
questions.explanation: A large gap between training (high) and validation (low) scores is high variance (overfitting). The fix is a simpler model, more regularization, or techniques like dropout -- not more data if the gap persists.

questions.question: AUC-ROC = 0.5 for a binary classifier. What does this indicate?
options: The model perfectly separates the two classes across every possible decision threshold
The model has exactly 50% accuracy on the evaluation set regardless of the chosen threshold
The model performs no better than random guessing at ranking positives above negatives
The model has equal precision and recall values at its default classification threshold
questions.explanation: AUC-ROC = 0.5 means the model's ranking of positive and negative examples is no better than random. AUC = 1.0 would be perfect separation. The metric is threshold-independent.

questions.question: What is the best completion criterion for Model Evaluation?
options: Compute precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC, and regression metrics (MSE, RMSE, MAE, R-squared) from scratch
Skip validation and trust the first plausible-looking output
Choose a production framework before defining the core mechanism, with no need to inspect intermediate results or test edge cases
Treat one successful example as proof that every edge case works
questions.explanation: “Compute precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC, and regression metrics (MSE, RMSE, MAE, R-squared) from scratch” is one of this lesson’s stated outcomes; the other choices bypass its required reasoning or validation.
